title: Holding Others Accountable Starts With the Leader
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that before a leader disciplines an underperforming team member, the leader has diagnostic work to do. It walks through the many reasons a person might fail at a task — missing skills, distraction, inexperience, unclear expectations, or a mismatched standard — and insists that leaders are usually the first party accountable for that failure, not the employee. Only in the narrower case of a genuine deficit in self-discipline or commitment does the piece treat accountability as squarely the team member's problem. The framing positions great leaders as teachers first, correcting outcomes by first correcting their own preparation and clarity. It closes by describing accountability, done well, as an act of reflection rather than blame.
points: Leaders should diagnose the root cause of underperformance (skills, distraction, experience, standards, commitment) before assigning blame.
In most cases the leader, not the team member, is the first party accountable for a performance failure because leaders set standards and provide the tools to succeed.
The exception is a genuine failure of self-discipline or commitment — in that narrower case, accountability shifts squarely to the individual.
Weaponizing accountability by simply demanding better performance, without examining the leader's own role, is a mark of poor leadership.
quotes: Holding that team member accountable for improvement is what leaders are required to do.
As you can imagine after reading that abbreviated list, what a leader does to encourage future improvement varies widely depending on the reasons for the poor performance.
Leaders, by definition, are obligated to set the standards, clarify expectations, set priorities, and give team members the skills and experience to succeed.
Unfortunately, holding others accountable for attitude, commitment, or self-discipline is usually a losing proposition.
Good leaders don’t weaponize accountability for failure by simply demanding better performance.
The reflection of both the cause and the solution starts in that mirror.
